newsitem.title: USA: W.House, Congress reach tentative budget deal.
newsitem.headline: W.House, Congress reach tentative budget deal.

text.p: White House officials and Senate Republicans said on Monday they had reached a tentative agreement to cut taxes and balance the budget by 2002.
"We have reached tentative agreement with the administration on the balanced budget ... and tax cut package," Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott told a hurriedly assembled news conference.
In Las Vegas, a White House spokesman said President Bill Clinton was happy with the deal.

"The president was pleased with the information and was looking forward to a full briefing in the morning," White House spokesman Joe Lockhart told reporters in Las Vegas, where Clinton was wrapping up a three-day trip to the Western United States.

Lockhart said that White House Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles had called an aide who was with the president and told him that a tentative deal had been reached. At 4:30 p.m. PDT (7:30 EDT) the aide reached Clinton on the golf course at the Las Vegas Country Club, where the president was golfing with basketball superstar Michael Jordan and some state governors.
Clinton sought and received assurances that three issues had been taken care of: more spending for education, a child tax credit, and an expansion of health benefits for poor children, Lockhart said.
The historic agreement reached on Monday to balance the U.S. budget by 2002 followed years of wrangling between Clinton and congressional Republicans over taxing and spending priorities.

Republican leaders and top administration officials have been closeted in Lott's office for most of the day working out a final deal on a plan to balance the budget by 2002 and cut taxes by at least $85 billion over five years. Congressional sources have said this net tax cut could rise over $90 billion once the final numbers are calculated.

Clinton, in Las Vegas to speak to the nation's governors, had said earlier on Monday that the two sides were on the verge of an agreement and Republican leaders were equally optimistic that it could be finalised on Monday.
"This is an historic opportunity. It can be the achievement of a generation," Clinton said.
Monday's agreement will allow lawmakers in the House and the Senate to vote on the budget and tax bills before they leave on Friday for a month-long vacation.
Lott said the Senate would vote on the spending bill on Wednesday and consider the tax bill on Thursday.

Once enacted, the plan would give taxpayers the first tax cut in 16 years, a $85 billion tax break that would include a $500-per-child tax credit, expand retirement accounts, help pay for higher education and lower taxes on capital gains.
The plan would balance the budget by 2002, or before, and would restructure several health care programmes, including taking $115 billion from the Medicare programme for senior citizens.
